**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I realized words could carry weight, I was twelve. My father had just left, and my mother sat me down at the kitchen table, her hands trembling around a cup of tea that had long gone cold. She said, *"Words are like stones. Once you throw them, you can’t take them back."* I didn’t understand then. I thought words were just sounds, fleeting things that disappeared into the air. But that night, I lay awake, replaying every harsh word I’d ever said to him—*You’re never here. You don’t care. You’re just like everyone else.* And I wondered if those words had been the ones that finally broke him.

Years later, I found myself standing in front of a blank page, a pen hovering over paper. I was supposed to write something profound, something that would make people feel. But all I could think about was the weight of those words I’d thrown at my father. Had they landed? Had they bruised him the way his absence had bruised me? I wrote a single sentence: *"I’m sorry."* Then I crumpled the paper and threw it away.

Words are funny like that. They can build bridges or burn them down. They can heal or wound. They can be the difference between a life lived in silence and one shouted from the rooftops. But the most dangerous thing about words is that they don’t always mean what we intend. A compliment can sound like mockery. A joke can cut deeper than a knife. And sometimes, the words we don’t say are the heaviest of all.

I think about the things I never told my father. That I missed him. That I understood, even if I didn’t want to. That I loved him, even when he wasn’t there. But those words stayed locked inside me, too heavy to lift. And now, they’re just echoes in an empty house.

So I write. Not because I have anything profound to say, but because words are the only way I know how to measure the weight of what’s left unsaid. And maybe, just maybe, if I throw them carefully enough, they’ll land where they’re meant to.
